name: United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (2026-2030)

children.name: By 2030 public institutions and the private sector catalyze gender responsive, climate-resilient and sustainable green growth promoting social equity and decent jobs

1.1 Authorities develop and implement legislation, policy and regulatory frameworks for a diversified, green, circular, and climate-resilient economy, that is gender-inclusive, with stronger management of biodiversity, natural and cultural resources

1.2 Authorities, the private sector and communities have enhanced capacities, including financial and nonfinancial support, to develop an inclusive, greener, and productive business sector and improve livelihoods

1.3 Authorities and the private sector address the skills mismatch and shortages, with stronger active labour market measures to increase participation rates, particularly for women, youth, migrant workers and persons at risk of being left behind.

1.4 Authorities and the private sector have increased capacities for sustainable management of energy resources, natural resources, biodiversity, infrastructure and waste, and effective climate, emergency and disaster resilience and response.

1.5 Authorities and private sector foster a gender-responsive environment enabling women’s economic participation through access to jobs, voluntary work, entrepreneurship, equitable pay, and care services.

1.6 Communities and individuals are empowered to actively participate in climate change adaptation, preparation and mitigation measures to cope with the risks and impact of disasters and climate-induced displacement

By 2030 people, especially persons at risk of being left behind, including persons with disabilities, benefit from improved quality and inclusive education, lifelong learning opportunities, and enhanced, gender-responsive health and social protection systems

2.1 Service providers have improved tools, capacities, and evidence-based policy frameworks and financing to deliver multi-sectoral programmes for all, especially for persons at risk of being left behind, including on GBV and VAC.
2.2 Authorities have advanced digital transformation in education, health and social protection systems for efficient delivery of services.
2.3 People, including persons at risk of being left behind, have improved access to information and means to claim their rights to education, social protection and health services.

2.4 Authorities have increased capacities to develop policy frameworks and deliver more efficient, resilient, inclusive, and gender-responsive health, One Health, nutrition and early childhood development systems.
2.5 Authorities have improved policies, systems, and institutional capacities to advance inclusive and quality education.
2.6 Authorities have enhanced capacities to strengthen lifelong learning systems, including technical and vocational education and training.
2.7 Social protection systems are strengthened to deliver more inclusive services, with expanded coverage and a focus on populations at risk of being left behind.
By 2030 people contribute to and benefit from more effective and accountable institutions, fostering gender equality, youth empowerment, peace and social cohesion
3.1 Institutions have policies and mechanisms in place to enable effective civic engagement in policy and service design, delivery and monitoring.

3.2 Communities and civil society, especially women, youth and those representing persons at risk of being left behind have enhanced capacities, resources, and access to platforms that enable them to exercise their rights and meaningfully participate in decision-making processes.

3.3 Institutions, communities and civil society have the capabilities to foster social cohesion, promote trust, ensure gender equality, youth empowerment and protect human rights, contributing to peaceful and inclusive society.

3.4 Public, private, and civil society actors are equipped with the knowledge and tools to advance human rights, gender-transformative leadership, and develop gender-responsive institutions, policies, and practices.

3.5 Institutions, including the judiciary and law enforcement agencies, have strengthened capacities and enabling conditions to enhance human security and access to services, justice, the rule of law and the protection of human rights.

3.6 Institutions have enhanced capacities to apply good governance and gender-responsive governance, and leverage digital, innovative and financial solutions to advance sustainable development and eradicate corruption.

projects.name: 1.1.11 Culture and creativity harnessed for sustainable development
projects.description:
Activities will entail the development of three museums and two culture and creative hubs. More concretely this implies the
•	construction, reconstruction and rehabilitation of buildings where these facilities will operate, 
•	development of professional capacities of existing and future employees with respecting gender balance and focusing on youth, as well as 
•	equipping the facilities with new equipment and tools, also digital, for successful management of collections, audio-visual processes, and 
•	other planned activities.
The output would lead to improved protection and management of cultural heritage, and development of creative industries, while the outcomes would support progress towards reconciliation and good neighborly relations within and outside Bosnia and Herzegovina through the promotion of cultural diversity.

projects.name: 1.4.6 Capacities to implement obligations under the Montreal Protocol strengthened
projects.description:
The main objective of institutional strengthening is to establish a national institutional mechanism for coordinating national and international efforts to protect the ozone layer, with a particular focus on facilitating the accelerated phase-out of ozone-depleting substances. In its current phase, the institutional strengthening project focuses on building national capacity and reinforcing regulatory efforts to ensure compliance with upcoming hydrochlorofluorocarbon (HCFC) consumption phase-out targets. Key activities include monitoring the promulgation and enforcement of policies and legislation introducing additional restrictions on HCFCs; strengthening cooperation with the customs authorities to prevent illegal trade in controlled substances and with refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment associations; and continuing implementation of stage II of the hydrochlorofluorocarbon phase-out management plan (HPMP).

The project also supports the upgrading of the hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) outlook model and the preparation of the project proposal for the Kigali implementation plan for HFCs. In parallel, awareness-raising activities and participation in regional and international meetings are being continued. Coordination is being strengthened with climate authorities on the inclusion of fluorinated gases in nationally determined contributions, as well as with authorities responsible for safety standards and energy efficiency. Gender mainstreaming is integrated across all aspects of the institutional strengthening project implementation.
